by: claude-sonnet-5-5, in a Claude Code session

subtopics.title: de Broglie waves and wavelength
subtopics.theory_md:
**de Broglie hypothesis:** every moving particle has a wave of wavelength $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{p}=\dfrac{h}{mv}$, $h=6.626\times10^{-34}$ J s. (Davisson-Germer: electron diffraction from a nickel crystal confirmed it.)

For a charge $q$ accelerated from rest through $V$: $qV=\dfrac{p^2}{2m}$, so $\lambda=\dfrac{h}{\sqrt{2mqV}}$.
- Electron: $\lambda=\dfrac{12.27}{\sqrt V}$ Å
- Proton: $\lambda\approx\dfrac{0.286}{\sqrt V}$ Å

Equal $\lambda$ means equal momentum. Large $m$ or $v$ gives a tiny $\lambda$, so everyday objects show no wave nature.
subtopics.basics_md: Light is both wave and particle. de Broglie said matter is too: the faster or heavier the thing, the shorter its wave, which is why a cricket ball shows no waves but an electron does.

questions.q: The de Broglie wavelength of a particle of mass $m$ and speed $v$ is
questions.why: $\lambda=h/p$ and $p=mv$.

questions.q: An electron and a proton are accelerated through the same potential difference. The shorter de Broglie wavelength belongs to the
options: proton, as its momentum is larger
electron, as it has more charge
questions.why: $\lambda=h/\sqrt{2mqV}$: same $q$ and $V$, larger $m$ gives smaller $\lambda$. Students wrongly think a lighter particle has a shorter wave.

questions.q: An electron is accelerated from rest through 50 V. Find its de Broglie wavelength.
What potential difference is needed to give an electron a de Broglie wavelength of 1.0 Å? What is its kinetic energy?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Formula.** $\lambda=\dfrac{12.27}{\sqrt V}$ Å, so $\sqrt V=12.27$ for $\lambda=1.0$ Å.

$V=(12.27)^2=150.6$ V $\approx 1.5\times10^2$ V

**Kinetic energy** $=eV\approx150$ eV.

points: Hypothesis: moving particle has a wave, $\lambda=h/p=h/mv$ (1)

subtopics.title: Wave packet, phase and group velocity
subtopics.theory_md:
A particle is a **wave packet**: a group of waves of slightly different $k$ that interfere constructively only in a small region $\Delta x$ and cancel elsewhere. A single plane wave fills all space, so it cannot describe a localised particle.

- Phase velocity $v_p=\dfrac{\omega}{k}$ (speed of one crest).
- Group velocity $v_g=\dfrac{d\omega}{dk}$ (speed of the packet envelope, equals particle velocity $v$).

From $\omega=kv_p$: $v_g=v_p+k\dfrac{dv_p}{dk}=v_p-\lambda\dfrac{dv_p}{d\lambda}$. With no dispersion $v_g=v_p$.

Matter wave: $\hbar\omega=mc^2$, $\hbar k=mv$, so $v_p=\dfrac{c^2}{v}$ and $v_pv_g=c^2$. Since $v<c$, $v_p>c$, allowed because no energy travels at $v_p$.
subtopics.basics_md: A crowd doing a wave in a stadium: the pattern travels at one speed (phase), while a bunch of tall people in the pattern, the packet, can move at another (group). The particle goes with the bunch.
key_points: Wave packet: superposition of waves of nearby $k$, localised in $\Delta x$

questions.q: Group velocity of a wave packet is
questions.why: $v_g=d\omega/dk$; $\omega/k$ is the phase velocity.

questions.q: For a de Broglie wave of a particle moving at speed $v<c$, the phase velocity is
questions.why: $v_p=\omega/k=mc^2/mv=c^2/v$. It exceeds $c$ but carries no energy, so relativity is not violated.

questions.q: What is a wave packet? Why is a single plane wave not enough to represent a particle?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Wave packet.** A group of waves with slightly different wave numbers $k$ (a spread $\Delta k$) that superpose, reinforcing in a small region $\Delta x$ and cancelling outside it.

**Why not a plane wave.** A plane wave $e^{i(kx-\omega t)}$ has a definite $k$ and $|\psi|^2$ is constant everywhere, so the particle would be equally likely to be anywhere ($\Delta x=\infty$). A particle is localised, so it needs a packet. Localising it makes $\Delta k$ large, consistent with $\Delta x\,\Delta k\ge\tfrac12$.
points: Definition: superposition of waves of nearby $k$, localised
Plane wave has definite $k$ and uniform $|\psi|^2$, not localised

questions.q: An electron moves at $2\times10^6$ m/s. Find the phase velocity of its de Broglie wave. Take $c=3\times10^8$ m/s. Comment on the result.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Formula.** $v_p=\dfrac{c^2}{v}$

$v_p=\dfrac{(3\times10^8)^2}{2\times10^6}=4.5\times10^{10}$ m/s

**Comment.** $v_p>c$ (150 times). This is allowed: the energy and the particle travel at the group velocity $v_g=v=2\times10^6$ m/s, and $v_pv_g=c^2$.

points: Two close waves added: envelope $\cos\frac{\Delta\omega t-\Delta kx}{2}$ moves at $\Delta\omega/\Delta k\to d\omega/dk$
Wave packet: group of waves, moves at $v_g$ equal to particle velocity

subtopics.title: Heisenberg uncertainty principle
subtopics.theory_md:
Position and momentum cannot both be known exactly:
$$\Delta x\,\Delta p\ge\frac{\hbar}{2}=\frac{h}{4\pi}$$
and similarly $\Delta E\,\Delta t\ge\hbar/2$. It is a property of waves (a narrow packet needs a wide spread of $k$), not a flaw of the instrument.

**Estimate type:** a particle confined to a region of size $\Delta x$ has $\Delta p_{min}=\dfrac{h}{4\pi\,\Delta x}$ and $\Delta v=\Delta p/m$.

Use $h=6.626\times10^{-34}$ J s, $m_e=9.11\times10^{-31}$ kg. Note: some books use $\Delta x\Delta p\ge h/2\pi$ or $h$; the paper's answer used $h/4\pi$.
subtopics.basics_md: Pin a wave down to a tiny spot and it must be made of many different wavelengths, so its momentum becomes uncertain. Squeezing position always costs certainty in momentum.
key_points: Smaller region gives larger $\Delta p$ and $\Delta v=\Delta p/m$
Consequence of wave nature, forces zero-point energy

questions.q: If the position of an electron is known more precisely, the uncertainty in its momentum
questions.why: $\Delta p\ge\hbar/2\Delta x$: smaller $\Delta x$ forces larger $\Delta p$.

questions.q: Which pair obeys an uncertainty relation?
questions.why: $\Delta E\,\Delta t\ge\hbar/2$.

questions.q: An electron is confined to a region of width 0.1 nm. Estimate the minimum uncertainty in its momentum and velocity.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Given.** $\Delta x=10^{-10}$ m.

$\Delta p_{min}=\dfrac{h}{4\pi\Delta x}=\dfrac{6.626\times10^{-34}}{4\pi\times10^{-10}}=5.27\times10^{-25}$ kg m/s

$\Delta v=\dfrac{\Delta p}{m}=\dfrac{5.27\times10^{-25}}{9.11\times10^{-31}}=5.8\times10^{5}$ m/s

subtopics.title: Schrodinger equation and the wave function
subtopics.theory_md:
The wave function $\psi$ carries everything about the particle. **Born interpretation:** $|\psi|^2$ is the probability density; $P(a<x<b)=\int_a^b|\psi|^2dx$.

**Time-dependent:** $i\hbar\dfrac{\partial\psi}{\partial t}=-\dfrac{\hbar^2}{2m}\dfrac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial x^2}+V\psi$

**Time-independent** (steady states, $\psi(x,t)=\psi(x)e^{-iEt/\hbar}$):
$$\frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2}+\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}(E-V)\psi=0$$
It comes from $E=\dfrac{p^2}{2m}+V$ with $p\to-i\hbar\,\partial/\partial x$ and $E\to i\hbar\,\partial/\partial t$.
subtopics.basics_md: Newton's law tells a ball's path. For an electron, Schrodinger's equation tells its wave, and the square of the wave tells where you are likely to find it.

questions.q: The physical meaning of $|\psi(x)|^2$ is
options: the probability per unit length of finding the particle at $x$
questions.why: Born interpretation.

questions.q: In the time-independent Schrodinger equation, $E-V$ is the particle's
questions.why: $E=T+V$, so $E-V=T$.

questions.q: Derive the one-dimensional time-independent Schrodinger equation for a particle of mass $m$ in a potential $V(x)$.
questions.model_answer_md:
**1. Wave function.** A free particle: $\psi=Ae^{i(kx-\omega t)}$, with $p=\hbar k$, $E=\hbar\omega$.

**2. Differentiate.** $\dfrac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial x^2}=-k^2\psi=-\dfrac{p^2}{\hbar^2}\psi$, so $p^2\psi=-\hbar^2\dfrac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial x^2}$.

**3. Energy.** Total energy $E=\dfrac{p^2}{2m}+V$. Multiply by $\psi$:
$$E\psi=-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m}\frac{\partial^2\psi}{\partial x^2}+V\psi$$

**4. Steady state.** For a stationary state $\psi(x,t)=\psi(x)e^{-iEt/\hbar}$, the time factor cancels:
$$\boxed{\frac{d^2\psi}{dx^2}+\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}(E-V)\psi=0}$$
points: Final equation with time factor removed

subtopics.title: Acceptable wave functions and normalisation
subtopics.theory_md:
An acceptable $\psi$ must be **single-valued, finite, continuous** (with continuous $d\psi/dx$ except where $V=\infty$) and **square-integrable**.

**Normalisation:** $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}|\psi|^2dx=1$ (particle is somewhere). Find the constant $A$ from this.

**Probability** in $a<x<b$: $\int_a^b|\psi|^2dx$ with $\psi$ normalised.

Tests: $e^{x^2}$ blows up at infinity; $\tan x$, $\cot x$ have infinities; $e^{-x}$ on $0<x<\infty$ is fine. Useful: $\int\cos^2x\,dx=\frac x2+\frac{\sin2x}{4}$.
subtopics.basics_md: All the probability must add up to 1, like slices of a pie. If the wave function is infinite somewhere or never dies away, you cannot scale it to total 1, so it cannot describe a real particle.
key_points: State which condition fails and give the reason

questions.q: Which function is an acceptable wave function on $-\infty<x<\infty$?
questions.why: Only $e^{-x^2}$ is finite and square-integrable. $x$ and $e^x$ diverge; $\tan x$ has infinities.

questions.q: A particle has $\psi=Ax$ for $0<x<1$ and 0 elsewhere. The normalisation constant $A$ is
questions.why: $A^2\int_0^1x^2dx=A^2/3=1$, so $A=\sqrt3$. The common error is to forget the square.

questions.q: For $\psi=Ax$ ($0<x<1$, zero elsewhere) find $A$ and the probability of finding the particle between $x=0$ and $x=0.5$.

points: $\tan x$ is infinite at $\pm\pi/2,\dots$ and cannot be normalised

subtopics.title: Particle in a box: levels and wave function
subtopics.theory_md:
**Setup:** $V=0$ for $0<x<L$, $V=\infty$ outside, so $\psi=0$ at $x=0$ and $x=L$.

Inside: $\psi''+k^2\psi=0$, $k^2=\dfrac{2mE}{\hbar^2}$, so $\psi=A\sin kx+B\cos kx$.
- $\psi(0)=0\Rightarrow B=0$
- $\psi(L)=0\Rightarrow kL=n\pi$, $n=1,2,3,\dots$ ($n=0$ gives $\psi=0$)

$$E_n=\frac{n^2h^2}{8mL^2},\qquad p_n=\frac{nh}{2L}$$
Normalising, $A^2\dfrac L2=1$: $\psi_n=\sqrt{\dfrac2L}\sin\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}$. Levels go as $n^2$ (spacing grows), $\psi_n$ has $n-1$ nodes, $E\propto1/L^2$.
subtopics.basics_md: A guitar string pinned at both ends can only vibrate with whole numbers of half-waves. A confined particle's wave is pinned the same way, so only certain wavelengths, hence certain energies, are allowed.
key_points: Narrower box: larger energies and spacing

questions.q: The energy levels of a particle in an infinite 1-D well are proportional to
The width of an infinite well is doubled. The ground-state energy becomes
questions.why: $E_1\propto1/L^2$, so doubling $L$ divides $E_1$ by 4. Students often say half.

questions.q: State the boundary conditions for a particle in a 1-D infinite well and show how they lead to $E_n=n^2h^2/8mL^2$.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Boundary conditions.** $\psi(0)=0$ and $\psi(L)=0$ (infinite walls, particle cannot be outside).

**Solution.** Inside, $\psi=A\sin kx+B\cos kx$ with $k^2=2mE/\hbar^2$.
- $\psi(0)=0\Rightarrow B=0$.
- $\psi(L)=0\Rightarrow\sin kL=0\Rightarrow k=n\pi/L$.

$$E_n=\frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m}=\frac{n^2\pi^2\hbar^2}{2mL^2}=\frac{n^2h^2}{8mL^2}$$

questions.q: The ground-state wave function of a well is $\psi_1=\sqrt{2/L}\sin(\pi x/L)$. Find the probability of finding the particle in the middle third, $L/3<x<2L/3$.

points: $E_n=n^2h^2/8mL^2$; levels $E_1,4E_1,9E_1$: quantised by the boundary conditions
Uncertainty principle: confinement forces $\Delta p\ge\hbar/2L$, minimum $E_1=h^2/8mL^2$

subtopics.title: Zero-point energy
subtopics.theory_md:
**Zero-point energy** is the minimum, non-zero energy of a bound particle. In the box, $E_1=\dfrac{h^2}{8mL^2}>0$. The state $n=0$ would give $\psi\equiv0$, i.e. no particle.

**Uncertainty-principle reason:** confinement to $\Delta x\approx L$ gives $\Delta p\ge\dfrac{\hbar}{2L}$, so the particle cannot be at rest and has kinetic energy.

Harmonic oscillator: $E_0=\tfrac12\hbar\omega$.

**Importance:** atoms and molecules keep vibrating at 0 K; liquid helium does not freeze at atmospheric pressure even at 0 K; the electron does not fall into the nucleus (that would need tiny $\Delta x$ and huge $\Delta p$).
subtopics.basics_md: If a particle sat perfectly still in a small room, you would know both where it is and that its momentum is zero. Nature forbids that, so there is always some leftover motion.
key_points: Consequences: vibration at 0 K, helium liquid, atomic stability

questions.q: The zero-point energy of a particle in an infinite 1-D well of width $L$ is
questions.why: The lowest state is $n=1$.

questions.q: Why can a particle in an infinite well not have zero energy?
options: energy is always positive by definition
$n=0$ makes the wave function zero everywhere
questions.why: With $n=0$, $\psi=A\sin0=0$, so the particle would not exist. The uncertainty principle gives the physical reason.

questions.q: Explain, using the uncertainty principle, why an electron confined in a box has non-zero minimum energy. Estimate it for width $L$.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Argument.** Confining the electron to width $L$ gives $\Delta x\approx L$. Then $\Delta p\ge\dfrac{\hbar}{2L}$, so the electron cannot be at rest.

**Estimate.** $E_{min}\sim\dfrac{(\Delta p)^2}{2m}=\dfrac{\hbar^2}{8mL^2}$ (same $1/L^2$ dependence as the exact $E_1=\dfrac{h^2}{8mL^2}$).

Narrower box gives larger $\Delta p$ and larger zero-point energy.

points: No, zero energy is not allowed
Zero-point energy is the minimum non-zero energy, $E_1=h^2/8mL^2$, $E_0=\hbar\omega/2$
From uncertainty principle: cannot be at rest
Consequences: vibration at 0 K, liquid helium, electron does not collapse into nucleus

subtopics.title: Particle in a box: numericals
subtopics.theory_md:
Work in SI, convert at the end ($1$ eV $=1.602\times10^{-19}$ J).

- Energy: $E_n=\dfrac{n^2h^2}{8mL^2}$; momentum $p_n=\dfrac{nh}{2L}$.
- Ratio problems: $E\propto n^2$ and $E\propto1/L^2$, so $\dfrac{E_2}{E_1}=\dfrac{L_1^2}{L_2^2}$ for the same state.
- Photon from a jump $n_i\to n_f$: $h\nu=E_i-E_f$, $\lambda=\dfrac{hc}{\Delta E}=\dfrac{1240\ \text{eV nm}}{\Delta E\ (\text{eV})}$.
- Probability: $P=\dfrac2L\int\sin^2\dfrac{n\pi x}{L}dx$; the antiderivative is $\dfrac xL-\dfrac{1}{2n\pi}\sin\dfrac{2n\pi x}{L}$. A symmetric state gives $1/2$ for either half.

Electron in a 1 nm box: $E_1=0.376$ eV.
subtopics.basics_md: Plug into $E_n=n^2h^2/8mL^2$, keep units straight (metres, kilograms), and for probabilities integrate $|\psi|^2$ over the interval.

questions.q: The ground-state energy of an electron in a 1 nm infinite well is about
questions.why: $E_1=h^2/8mL^2=6.02\times10^{-20}$ J $=0.376$ eV. Wrong options come from slipping a power of ten in $L$.

questions.q: In a symmetric infinite well, the probability of finding the particle in the first half ($0<x<L/2$) for any state $n$ is
questions.why: $|\psi_n|^2$ is symmetric about $L/2$ for every $n$.

questions.q: An electron is in an infinite well of width 1 nm. Find $E_1$, $E_2$ and the wavelength of the photon emitted in the $n=2\to n=1$ transition.
An electron in an infinite well has $E_1=1.50$ eV for width $L_1$. The well is narrowed to $L_1/2$. What are the new $E_1$ and the new $E_3$?

subtopics.title: Quantum harmonic oscillator: energy levels
subtopics.theory_md:
Potential $V=\tfrac12kx^2=\tfrac12m\omega^2x^2$, $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$. Solving the Schrodinger equation $\psi''+\dfrac{2m}{\hbar^2}\left(E-\tfrac12m\omega^2x^2\right)\psi=0$ gives
$$E_n=\left(n+\tfrac12\right)\hbar\omega=\left(n+\tfrac12\right)h\nu,\quad n=0,1,2,\dots$$
- Levels are **equally spaced** by $\hbar\omega$ (box: spacing grows).
- **Zero-point energy** $E_0=\tfrac12\hbar\omega$ (lowest, not zero).
- Ground state $\psi_0\propto e^{-m\omega x^2/2\hbar}$ (Gaussian); $\psi_n$ has $n$ nodes.
- Selection rule for transitions: $\Delta n=\pm1$.
subtopics.basics_md: A mass on a spring, but quantised: it can only have energies half a step, one and a half steps, two and a half steps, and so on, with equal steps of $\hbar\omega$. It never fully stops.

questions.q: The ground-state energy of a quantum harmonic oscillator of angular frequency $\omega$ is
questions.why: $E_0=(0+\frac12)\hbar\omega$.

questions.q: The energy difference between adjacent levels of a harmonic oscillator is
questions.why: Equal spacing is the signature; students confuse it with the box, where spacing grows with $n$.

questions.q: A molecule vibrates as a harmonic oscillator with $\omega=2.0\times10^{14}$ rad/s. Find its zero-point energy and the energy of the first excited state in eV.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\hbar=1.0546\times10^{-34}$ J s

$E_0=\tfrac12\hbar\omega=\tfrac12(1.0546\times10^{-34})(2.0\times10^{14})=1.05\times10^{-20}$ J $=0.066$ eV

$E_1=\tfrac32\hbar\omega=0.197$ eV

(Spacing $\hbar\omega=0.132$ eV.)

questions.q: Write the energy of a linear harmonic oscillator and discuss its zero-point energy and spacing. How does it differ from the infinite well?
questions.model_answer_md:
**Energy.** $E_n=(n+\tfrac12)\hbar\omega$, $n=0,1,2,\dots$

**Zero-point energy.** $E_0=\tfrac12\hbar\omega\ne0$: from the uncertainty principle, the oscillator cannot sit at rest at $x=0$ (that would fix both $x$ and $p$).

**Spacing.** Equal, $\hbar\omega$.

**Contrast with the well.**
- Box: $E_n\propto n^2$, spacing grows with $n$; oscillator: $E_n$ linear in $n$, spacing constant.
- Box: lowest level $h^2/8mL^2$; oscillator: $\hbar\omega/2$.

subtopics.title: Quantum vs classical oscillator
subtopics.theory_md:
**Classical:** energy is continuous, can be zero (particle at rest at $x=0$); the particle never goes beyond the turning points $x=\pm A$ where $\tfrac12kA^2=E$; it is fastest at the centre, so most likely found near the ends.

**Quantum:**
- Energy is discrete, $E_n=(n+\tfrac12)\hbar\omega$; never zero.
- $\psi$ extends **beyond the classical turning points** (it decays exponentially there): the particle can be found in a classically forbidden region.
- Ground state: highest probability at the centre. For large $n$ the quantum probability averages to the classical one (correspondence principle).

Link to spring: $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$, $\nu=\omega/2\pi$.
subtopics.basics_md: Classically a swing can have any energy and can rest at the bottom. Quantum mechanically it only takes specific energy steps, and its wave leaks slightly past where a classical swing would have to turn back.
key_points: Classical: continuous energy, can be zero, confined to $|x|\le A$

questions.q: Compared with a classical oscillator, the quantum oscillator's ground state
options: can be found outside the classical turning points
has zero probability at the centre
questions.why: $\psi_0$ is Gaussian and extends beyond the turning points.

questions.q: A spring-mass oscillator has $k=500$ N/m and $m=2.0$ kg. Its angular frequency is
questions.why: $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}=\sqrt{250}=15.8$ rad/s. Option 1 forgets the square root.

questions.q: Distinguish between a classical and a quantum harmonic oscillator.
questions.model_answer_md:
| | Classical | Quantum |
|---|---|---|
| Energy | continuous, can be 0 | $E_n=(n+\frac12)\hbar\omega$, discrete |
| Lowest energy | 0 (at rest) | $\hbar\omega/2$ |
| Motion limits | within $\pm A$ only | $\psi$ extends beyond $\pm A$ |
| Probability | highest near the ends | ground state highest at centre |

For large $n$ the quantum behaviour approaches the classical one.
points: Cannot vs can penetrate beyond turning points

questions.q: A diatomic molecule has effective spring constant $k=516$ N/m and reduced mass $1.67\times10^{-27}$ kg. Find its vibrational frequency $\nu$ and zero-point energy in eV.

subtopics.title: Quantum tunnelling through a barrier
subtopics.theory_md:
A particle of energy $E$ meets a barrier of height $V_0>E$ and width $a$. Classically it is always reflected. Quantum mechanically $\psi$ **decays exponentially** inside the barrier, does not vanish, and a small part emerges on the other side: **tunnelling**.

Inside the barrier: $\psi\propto e^{-\kappa x}$, $\kappa=\dfrac{\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}}{\hbar}$.

Transmission probability (thick barrier): $T\approx e^{-2\kappa a}$.
$T$ falls rapidly with larger $a$, larger $m$, larger $V_0-E$.

Applications: alpha decay, tunnel diode, scanning tunnelling microscope (STM), field emission, Josephson junction.
subtopics.basics_md: Throw a ball at a wall and it bounces. A wave, however, leaks a little way into the wall, and if the wall is thin enough some of the wave comes out the other side.
key_points: Uses: alpha decay, tunnel diode, STM

questions.q: Quantum tunnelling occurs when a particle crosses a barrier
options: by gaining energy from the barrier
only if its mass is large
questions.why: The wave function penetrates the barrier, giving non-zero transmission.

questions.q: If the barrier width is doubled, the transmission probability $T\approx e^{-2\kappa a}$
options: falls to the square of its old value
questions.why: $T_{new}=e^{-4\kappa a}=(e^{-2\kappa a})^2$.

questions.q: An electron of energy 2 eV meets a rectangular barrier of height 5 eV and width 0.5 nm. Estimate the transmission probability using $T\approx e^{-2\kappa a}$.
questions.model_answer_md:
$\kappa=\dfrac{\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}}{\hbar}=\dfrac{\sqrt{2(9.11\times10^{-31})(3\times1.602\times10^{-19})}}{1.0546\times10^{-34}}=8.87\times10^{9}$ m$^{-1}$

$2\kappa a=2(8.87\times10^{9})(0.5\times10^{-9})=8.87$

$T\approx e^{-8.87}=1.4\times10^{-4}$

(For 1 nm width, $T\approx2\times10^{-8}$: very sensitive to width, which is why STM works.)

questions.q: Explain quantum tunnelling and state the factors on which the transmission probability depends.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Tunnelling.** A particle of energy $E<V_0$ has a non-zero probability to cross a barrier. In the barrier $\psi$ decays exponentially, $\psi\propto e^{-\kappa x}$; if the barrier is thin the amplitude is still non-zero on the far side, so the particle appears there with probability $T$.

**Dependence.** $T\approx e^{-2\kappa a}$, $\kappa=\sqrt{2m(V_0-E)}/\hbar$:
- decreases with barrier width $a$,
- decreases with barrier height $V_0$ (increases with $E$),
- decreases with particle mass $m$.

subtopics.title: Alpha decay by tunnelling
subtopics.theory_md:
Inside a heavy nucleus (radius $R$) an alpha particle feels the strong nuclear attraction. Outside $R$ it feels the Coulomb repulsion $V(r)=\dfrac{2Ze^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0r}$, about 25 to 30 MeV high at $R$, while the alpha energy is only 4 to 9 MeV. Classically it can never escape.

**Gamow's theory:** it tunnels from $r=R$ to $r_0$, where $V(r_0)=E$:
$$T\approx e^{-2G},\quad G=\frac1\hbar\int_R^{r_0}\sqrt{2m[V(r)-E]}\,dr$$
It hits the barrier $f\approx v/2R$ times per second, so decay constant $\lambda=f\,e^{-2G}$.

$T$ is exponentially sensitive to $E$: half-lives range from $10^{-7}$ s to $10^{10}$ y (Geiger-Nuttall law).
subtopics.basics_md: The alpha is a prisoner rattling inside the nucleus. It does not have the energy to climb out, but its wave leaks through the wall, and each attempt has a tiny chance of success. Many attempts per second add up to the half-life.
key_points: Alpha energy (4-9 MeV) is below the Coulomb barrier (25-30 MeV)

questions.q: Alpha decay is explained as
options: alpha particle gaining energy from the electrons
questions.why: The alpha energy is below the barrier top.

questions.q: A small increase in the alpha particle energy changes the half-life
options: by a factor equal to the energy ratio
questions.why: $T\approx e^{-2G}$ with $G$ falling quickly as $E$ rises, hence the Geiger-Nuttall law.

questions.q: Explain why alpha decay cannot be understood classically, and how quantum tunnelling explains it.
questions.model_answer_md:
**Classical failure.** The Coulomb barrier at the nuclear surface is about 25 to 30 MeV but the alpha energy is only 4 to 9 MeV, so it cannot climb over.

**Quantum explanation.** The alpha's wave function decays inside the barrier but does not vanish, so there is a small probability $T\approx e^{-2G}$ to emerge at $r_0$ where $V=E$.

**Rate.** Decay constant $\lambda=f\,e^{-2G}$ with $f=v/2R$ attempts per second. $T$ is very sensitive to $E$, which explains the huge range of half-lives.

points: Tunnelling defined: particle crosses $V_0>E$ with non-zero probability, $\psi$ decays inside
Alpha in nucleus: nuclear attraction inside, Coulomb barrier $2Ze^2/4\pi\varepsilon_0r$ outside; barrier 25-30 MeV vs $E$ 4-9 MeV
